1.o: Mark's narrative does not take rise so early as those of Matthew and Luke do, from the birth of our Saviour, but from John's baptism, from which he soon passes to Christ's public ministry. Accordingly, in this chapter, we have, I. The office of John Baptist illustrated by the prophecy of him (ver. 1-3), and by the history of him, ver. 4-8. II. Christ's baptism, and his being owned from heaven, ver. 9-11. III. His temptation, ver. 12, 13. IV. His preaching, ver. 14, 15, 21, 22, 38, 39. V. His calling disciples, ver.
1.i: On one Sabbath in Capernaum Jesus taught with authority, freed a man, healed Peter's mother-in-law and many others, and rose early to pray.
1.p: Lord Jesus, You taught, healed and prayed. Teach us to begin each day with You. Amen.
1.l: Find a quiet moment early tomorrow, before the busy day starts, and talk to God.
q: Jesus began His next day by praying alone. How does your day begin?

2.o: In this chapter, we have, I. Christ's healing a man that was sick of a palsy, ver. 1-12. II. His calling of Matthew from the receipt of custom, and his eating, upon that occasion, with publicans and sinners, and justifying himself in so doing, ver. 13-17. III. His justifying his disciples in not fasting so much as those plucking the ears of corn on the sabbath day, ver. 23-28. All which passages we had before, Matt. ix. and xii.
2.i: Four friends lower a paralyzed man through a roof to Jesus, who forgives him and heals him.
2.p: Lord Jesus, You forgive and heal. Give us friends who bring us to You, and make us that kind of friend. Amen.
2.l: Help a friend today who needs a lift, and be willing to go to some trouble.
q: The man's friends carried him to Jesus and refused to give up. Who has carried you, and whom can you carry?

3.o: In this chapter, we have, I. Christ's healing a man that had a withered hand, on the sabbath day, and the combination of his enemies against him for it, ver. 1-6. II. The universal resort of people to him from all parts, to be healed, and the relief they all found with him, ver. 7-12. III. His ordaining his twelve apostles to be attendants on him, and the preachers of his gospel, ver. 13-21. IV.
3.i: On the Sabbath, in a synagogue, Jesus heals a man's withered hand while his critics watch and then plot against him.
3.p: Lord Jesus, You came to do good and to save. Soften our hard hearts, and make us glad when You heal. Amen.
3.l: Do one good thing for someone today, even if it is not the easy or expected thing.
q: The watchers cared more about the rule than about the man. When is that true for us?

4.o: In this chapter, we have, I. The parable of the seed, and the four sorts of ground (ver. 1-9), with the exposition of it (ver. 10-20), and the application of it, ver. 21-25. II. The parable of the seed growing gradually, but insensibly, ver. 26-29. III. The parable of the grain of mustard-seed, and a general account of Christ's parables, ver. 30-34. IV. The miracle of Christ's sudden stilling a storm at sea, ver. 35-41.
4.i: A storm threatens the disciples' boat while Jesus sleeps, and Jesus calms the wind and sea with a word.
4.p: Lord Jesus, You are in our boat. Calm our storms, and teach us to trust You. Amen.
4.l: The next time you are afraid, say, Jesus, You are in my boat, and take a slow breath.
q: Jesus slept in the storm, and the disciples panicked. What storm is Jesus asking you to trust Him in?

5.o: In this chapter, we have, I. Christ's casting the legion of devils out of the man possessed, and suffering them to enter into the swine, ver. 1-20. II. Christ's healing the woman with the bloody issue, in the way as he was going to raise Jairus's daughter to life, ver. 21-43. These three miracles we had the story of before (Matt. viii. 28, &c. and Matt. ix. 18, &c.) but more fully related here.
5.i: Jesus frees a man tormented by many spirits, sends the spirits into pigs, and sends the healed man home to tell his story.
5.p: Lord Jesus, You free those who are in chains. Thank You for setting us free, and help us tell others. Amen.
5.l: Tell someone today one thing Jesus has done for you, in your own words.
q: The healed man was told to go home and tell his story. Whom could you tell about Jesus?

6.o: A great variety of observable passages we have, in this chapter, concerning our Lord Jesus, the substance of all which we had before in Matthew, but divers circumstances we have, which we did not there meet with. Here is, I. Christ contemned by his countrymen, because he was one of them, and they knew, or thought they knew, his original, ver. 1-6. II. The just power he gave his apostles over unclean spirits, and an account given of their negotiation, ver. 7-13. III.
6.i: At Gennesaret, crowds bring the sick to Jesus and are healed by touching the fringe of his cloak.
6.p: Lord Jesus, we reach out to You. Heal us and those we love, and make us bring others to You. Amen.
6.l: Reach out to Jesus in prayer today with a need, even a small one, and trust Him with it.
q: People ran to bring their friends to Jesus. Who can you bring to Him today?

7.o: In this chapter we have, I. Christ's dispute with the scribes and Pharisees about eating meat with unwashen hands (ver. 1-13); and the needful instructions he gave to the people on that occasion, and further explained to his disciples, ver. 14-23. II. His curing of the woman Canaan's daughter that was possessed, ver. 24-30. III. The relief of a man that was deaf, and had an impediment in his speech, ver. 31-37.
7.i: Jesus took a deaf man aside, touched his ears and tongue, and with one Aramaic word, Ephphatha, opened his ears and loosed his speech.
7.p: Lord Jesus, open our ears to hear You and our mouths to speak of You. Amen.
7.l: Today, really listen to one person all the way to the end, without interrupting.
q: Jesus opened what was closed. What in you needs to be opened: your ears, your mouth, or your heart?

8.o: In this chapter, we have, I. Christ's miraculous feeding of four thousand with seven loaves and a few small fishes, ver. 1-9. II. His refusing to give the Pharisees a sign from heaven, ver. 10-13. III. His cautioning his disciples to take heed of the leaven of Pharisaism and Herodianism, ver. 14-21. IV. His giving of sight to a blind man at Bethsaida, ver. 22-26. V. Peter's confession of him, ver. 27-30. VI. The notice he gave his disciples of his own approaching sufferings (ver.
8.i: A second time Jesus fed a hungry crowd, this time from seven loaves and a few fish with seven baskets left over, showing that His care is not a one-time thing.
8.p: Lord Jesus, You see our needs before we ask. Thank You for daily bread, and make us generous. Amen.
8.l: At your next meal, thank God slowly, and think of someone who might be hungry. Ask God how you could help.
q: Jesus noticed that the people had been with Him three days and had nothing to eat. Who around you has been waiting, hungry, for someone to notice?

9.o: In this chapter, we have, I. Christ's transfiguration upon the mount, ver. 1-13. II. His casting the devil out of a child, when the disciples could not do it, ver. 14-29. III. His prediction of his own sufferings and death, ver. 30-32. IV. The check he gave to his disciples for disputing who should be greatest (ver. 33-37); and to John for rebuking one who cast out devils in Christ's name, and did not follow with them, ver. 38-41. V.
9.s: I Do Believe; Help My Unbelief
9.i: A father brought his sick son to Jesus, admitted he was torn between faith and doubt, and Jesus healed the boy and welcomed the honest prayer.
9.p: Lord Jesus, we believe; help our unbelief. Give us faith that turns to You in need. Amen.
9.l: Next time you doubt, tell Jesus honestly, like the father did: I believe, help my unbelief.
q: The scribes had no answer once Jesus arrived. When have you gone quiet because the right person finally walked in?

10.o: In this chapter, we have, I. Christ's dispute with the Pharisees concerning divorce, ver. 1-12. II. The kind entertainment he gave to the little children that were brought to him to be blessed, ver. 13-16. III. His trial of the rich man that enquired what he must do to get to heaven, ver. 17-22. IV. His discourse with his disciples, upon that occasion, concerning the peril of riches (ver. 23-27), and the advantage of being impoverished for his sake, ver. 28-31. V.
10.i: Mark 10 shows Jesus stopping His disciples from turning parents away, and then holding the children Himself.
10.p: Lord Jesus, You welcomed the children and held them close. Help us to come to You with open hands and trusting hearts. Amen.
10.l: Welcome someone younger than you today, and give them your full attention for a few minutes.
q: What would it look like for you to receive God's gifts with open hands, the way a child does?

11.o: We are now come to the Passion-Week, the week in which Christ died, and the great occurrences of that week. I. Christ's riding in triumph into Jerusalem, ver. 1-11. II. His cursing the barren fig-tree, ver. 12-14. III. His driving those out of the temple that turned it into an exchange, ver. 15-19. IV. His discourse with his disciples concerning the power of faith and the efficacy of prayer, on occasion of the withering of the fig-tree he cursed, ver. 20-26. V. His reply to those who questioned his authority, ver.
11.s: A House of Prayer for All Nations
11.i: Jesus drove out the buyers and sellers from the Temple court, quoting Isaiah that God's house is for all nations, and the leaders began plotting against Him.
11.p: Lord Jesus, Your house is a house of prayer for everyone. Clear out what crowds out our worship. Amen.
11.l: Make a quiet place for someone today: turn down the noise, or give someone room to pray or think.
q: Jesus cleared space for those who had no room to pray. Whom might you be crowding out?

12.o: In this chapter, we have, I. The parable of the vineyard let out to unthankful husbandmen, representing the sin and ruin of the Jewish church, ver. 1-12. II. Christ's silencing those who thought to ensnare him with a question about paying tribute Cæsar, ver. 13-17. III. His silencing the Sadducees, who attempted to perplex the doctrine of the resurrection, ver. 18-27. IV. His conference with a scribe about the first and great command of the law, ver. 28-34. V.
12.i: Pharisees and Herodians tried to trap Jesus with a question about taxes, and He answered with a coin and a principle: give Caesar his due and God His.
12.p: Lord Jesus, we belong to You. Help us to be honest citizens and faithful children of God. Amen.
12.l: Give something to God today that is truly yours, such as thanks, time, or a kind deed.
q: The coin carried Caesar's image, and people carry God's. What does it mean to give yourself back to Him?

13.o: We have here the substance of that prophetical sermon which our Lord Jesus preached, pointing at the destruction of Jerusalem, and the consummation of all things; it was one of the last of his sermons, and not ad populum—to the people, but ad clerum—to the clergy; it was private, preached only to four of his disciples, with whom his secret was. Here is, I. The occasion of his prediction—his disciples' admiring the building of the temple (ver.
13.s: The Fig Tree and the Signs
13.i: Mark 13 is the shortest account of Jesus' talk on the Mount of Olives, and it ends with one word: watch.
13.p: Lord, You told us to watch. Keep us alert, faithful in small things, and ready for Your return. Amen.
13.l: Pick something you can look after faithfully today, like a plant or a pet, and do it before anyone asks.
q: What impressive thing in your life are you leaning on?

14.o: In this chapter begins the account which this evangelist gives of the death and sufferings of our Lord Jesus, which we are all concerned to be acquainted, not only with the history of, but with the mystery of. Here is, I. The plot of the chief priests and scribes against Christ, ver. 1, 2. II. The anointing of Christ's head at a supper in Bethany, two days before his death, ver. 3-9. III. The contract Judas made with the chief priests, to betray him, ver. 10, 11. IV.
14.i: Mark 14 runs from a woman's gift in Bethany to the Passover table, the garden, the arrest, and Peter's failure, all in one long night.
14.p: Lord, You prayed alone while Your friends slept. Forgive us when we fail You, and keep us close to You. Amen.
14.l: If you have let someone down, tell them you are sorry today. Peter had to face what he did.
q: Gethsemane means an oil-press, a place where olives are crushed. What pressure has brought something good out of you?

15.o: What we read of the sufferings of Christ, in the foregoing chapter, was but the prologue or introduction; here we have the completing of them. We left him condemned by the chief priests; but they could only show their teeth, they could not bite. Here we have him, I. Arraigned and accused before Pilate the Roman governor, ver. 1-5. II. Cried out against by the common people, at the instigation of the priests, ver. 6-14. III. Condemned to be crucified immediately, ver. 15. IV.
15.i: Mark 15 is the shortest and starkest account of the cross, told in quick steps from morning to evening.
15.p: Lord Jesus, King on a cross, thank You for dying for us. Teach us to follow You with our whole hearts. Amen.
15.l: Tell someone today why you think Jesus is a king, or write down your reasons.
q: What fear are you avoiding that he has already walked through?

16.o: In this chapter, we have a short account of the resurrection and ascension of the Lord Jesus: and the joys and triumphs which it furnished all believers with, will be very acceptable to those who sympathised and suffered with Christ in the foregoing chapters. Here is, I. Christ's resurrection notified by an angel to the women that came to the sepulchre to anoint him, ver. 1-8. II. His appearance to Mary Magdalene, and the account she gave of it to the disciples, ver. 9-11. III.
16.i: Mark's Gospel ends, in its oldest copies, with eight short verses: women, a stone rolled away, and a young man with the news.
16.p: Risen Lord, You roll away the stones we cannot move. Fill us with Your joy and send us to tell it. Amen.
16.l: Tell someone today one thing that makes you glad because Jesus is alive.
q: Seasonable comfort comes to those who are looking for Jesus. What are you looking for in your grief?
